To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) during voluntary contraction of a human muscle, the recruitment of motor units occurs from small to large, as is the case during direct stimulation of nerves; 2) during electrically elicited muscle contraction, the recruitment order of the motor units is not necessarily the same as that observed during direct stimulation of a nerve, and 3) the conduction velocity of the muscle fibers and the spectral parameters of the electromyogram increase in a similar fashion with the level of the contraction, whether

1) conduction velocity and the two spectral parameters of the myoelectric signal increase with increasing voluntary contraction level, and 2) during electrical stimulation of the muscle motor point, conduction velocity increases in 72% and decreases in 28% of cases, while the spectral parameters show the same behavior in 50% of the cases.

The relationship between surface myo-electric signal parameters and the levels of voluntary and electrically induced contractions is complex and depends on the motor unit recruitment pattern and on the geometric location of each motor unit within the muscle.

the relationship between the level of contraction and the parameters of the surface myoelectric signals.

the recruitment order of motor units in a voluntary contraction is not always preserved when the muscle is electrically stimulated.

the use of surface myoelectric signals to infer motor unit recruitment order is not reliable.
the conduction velocity and the spectral parameters are not always reliable indicators of motor unit recruitment.
